This page summarises the method. The derivation and its checks are in the
report of the project the package grew out of (to be published).

## The model

Space is a set of $m$ areal units (districts, counties, grid cells) with an
adjacency graph; time is a regular grid of $T$ steps (months, quarters,
years). An *area-time cell* is one area in one time step. Surveys report
$y$ positives out of $k$ tested; surveys in the same cell are pooled, which
loses nothing because they share the same prevalence. For each observed
cell,

$$
y_{at} \sim \text{Binomial}\big(k_{at},\ \text{logit}^{-1}(x_{at})\big), \qquad
x_{at} = z_{at}^\top \beta + f_{at} + \epsilon_{at}.
$$

- $z_{at}^\top \beta$ are the **fixed effects**: an intercept, by default a
  linear trend in time (`trend()`, from $-1$ at the first step to $1$ at
  the last), and any covariates, which may vary by area, by time or by both.
  Their prior is Gaussian, $\beta \sim N(b_0, B)$.
- $f$ is a **Gaussian field** with separable covariance
  $\Sigma = \Sigma_t \otimes \Sigma_s$:
  - in space, a Leroux conditional autoregressive model on the graph, with
    precision $Q_s = \tau\{\rho_s R + (1 - \rho_s) I\}$, where $R = D - W$ is
    the graph Laplacian ($W$ the adjacency matrix, $D$ the numbers of
    neighbours), $\sigma^2 = 1/\tau$ sets the scale and $\rho_s \in (0, 1)$
    the strength of spatial dependence;
  - in time, a first-order autoregression with unit variance and lag-one
    correlation $\rho_t$.
- $\epsilon_{at} \sim N(0, \sigma_n^2)$ is a **cell-level nugget**: variation
  between surveys that the smooth field does not explain. It applies to the
  observed cells; the predicted surface is the field without it.

The hyperparameters $\theta = (\sigma, \rho_s, \rho_t, \sigma_n)$ have
half-normal and Beta priors (`areal_priors()`).

## Fitting on the observed cells only

Most area-time cells have no data: in the
[crt K76T tutorial](crt76t.html), 199 of 9,648. Because everything except
the likelihood is Gaussian, the unobserved cells can be integrated out
*exactly*: the $n$ observed cells' latent values $x_o$ have the Gaussian
prior

$$
x_o \sim N\big(Z_o b_0,\ \Sigma_{oo}\big), \qquad
\Sigma_{oo} = \Sigma_t[t_o, t_o] \circ \Sigma_s[a_o, a_o] + Z_o B Z_o^\top + \sigma_n^2 I,
$$

where $a_o$ and $t_o$ are the observed cells' areas and time steps and
$\circ$ is the elementwise product. The fixed effects are integrated out
too (the $Z_o B Z_o^\top$ term) and drawn afterwards from their exact
conditional distribution. The spatial block $\Sigma_s[a_o, a_o]$ comes from
a single eigendecomposition of $R$, done once when the frame is built, so
a change of $\tau$ or $\rho_s$ only rescales eigenvalues.

The MCMC therefore works on $n$ latent values, not $m \times T$, and its cost
per iteration grows as $n^3$, independently of the size of the full table.
This is what makes continental maps over decades feasible.

## The sampler

Each iteration updates the latent values, then the hyperparameters.

- **Latent values** by elliptical slice sampling (Murray, Adams & MacKay
  2010) against a *posterior-scaled* Gaussian (Nishihara, Murray & Adams
  2014): the Gaussian prior combined with a Gaussian approximation of each
  cell's likelihood (pseudo-data), with the approximation divided back out,
  so the update is exact. Proposing on this ellipse, rather than the
  prior's, is what lets heavily surveyed cells mix.
- **Hyperparameters** by two adaptive Metropolis moves: a centred move
  ($\theta$ given $x_o$) and the surrogate-data move of Murray & Adams
  (2010), in which $x_o$ moves with $\theta$. The centred move alone gets
  stuck, because $n$ latent values pin $\theta$.
- **During burn-in** the proposals adapt, and the pseudo-data are refitted
  twice to a Gaussian approximation of the likelihood at the chain's mean
  latent values. Both are then fixed, so the draws after burn-in come from
  an exact MCMC. The refit matters most for rare outcomes, where many cells
  have no positives.
- **Chains** start from dispersed points and run in parallel; `diagnose()`
  checks R-hat and effective sample sizes of every parameter, the latent
  value of every observed cell included.

## Prediction and aggregation

For each posterior draw of $(\theta, \beta, x_o)$, the full $m \times T$
surface is drawn by conditional simulation (Matheron's rule): an
unconditional draw of the field, corrected by kriging so that it agrees
with $x_o$. This is exact, and needs no matrix larger than $n \times n$
beyond the stored eigenvectors; the work is split into blocks of areas so
that memory stays bounded.

Each draw of the surface is then aggregated to any grouping of the areas
(regions, countries) as a weighted mean, and only then summarised. Group
estimates therefore carry the correlation between their areas, which
averaging area-level summaries would lose.

## Cross-validation

`crossval()` holds out folds of observed cells, refits, and predicts each
held-out cell from its exact conditional distribution given the fitted
cells, nugget included. The log predictive density integrates that
Gaussian against the binomial likelihood by adaptive Gauss-Hermite
quadrature, and calibration is checked with a randomised probability
integral transform.
